content.title: Sony-owned Crunchyroll faces class-action lawsuit for allegedly sharing private viewing data with marketin
content.text: Anime streaming platform Crunchyroll is facing a new class-action lawsuit in the United States over allegations that it improperly shared users’ private viewing habits and personal information with a third-party marketing company. The lawsuit claims the platform disclosed sensitive data, such as anime titles watched and user identifiers, without obtaining proper consent from subscribers.Filed in a federal court in California under the case Cabonios v. Crunchyroll, LLC, the complaint accuses the Sony-owned streaming service of violating privacy protections designed to safeguard consumer viewing records.The complaint lists Alicia Taylor, Anthony Gonzales, Francisco Cabonios, JT, Matthew Newton, and Oskar Toruno as plaintiffs. Allegations of sharing viewing habitsAccording to the lawsuit, Crunchyroll allegedly transmitted personally identifiable information to a marketing technology company called Braze, which provides tools for targeted advertising and customer engagement.Plaintiffs claim that the platform embedded a software development kit (SDK) from Braze in its mobile app. Through this integration, the app allegedly shared information which might extend to:Email addresses of usersUnique device identifiersDetails of specific anime titles and episodes being streamedLegal filings argue that the data allowed the marketing firm to build detailed behavioral profiles of subscribers and use them to send targeted notifications, in-app messages, and email campaigns based on viewing habits.The complaint further alleges that such disclosures have been occurring since at least 2022 without explicit and informed user consent.Possible violation of the Video Privacy Protection ActThe lawsuit centers on the Video Privacy Protection Act (VPPA), a US federal law enacted in 1988 to protect consumers’ video-watching history from being disclosed without permission.The VPPA prohibits companies classified as “video tape service providers” from knowingly sharing identifiable information about a consumer’s video viewing history unless the user provides clear, written consent.Under the statute, companies found in violation could face statutory damages of up to $2,500 per affected user, in addition to possible legal costs and other penalties.Previous privacy controversyThis is not the first time Crunchyroll has faced scrutiny over its data-privacy practices. In 2023, the company reached a $16 million settlement in a separate class-action lawsuit that also alleged violations of the VPPA through the sharing of user information with third-party analytics and advertising platforms.Although Crunchyroll denied wrongdoing in that case, it agreed to the settlement to avoid prolonged litigation and allowed eligible users to file claims for compensation.Plaintiffs in the new lawsuit argue that the alleged data-sharing practices are particularly concerning given that the company had already faced legal action over similar issues.Crunchyroll has not publicly responded in detail to the allegations at the time of reporting. If the case proceeds as a class action and plaintiffs succeed, the company could face significant financial liability depending on the number of affected users.
